slides.heading: Oral Lesson
bullets: In “A man who is rich owns that house,” there are really two statements joined together.
One is “A man owns that house”; the other is “who is rich” (that is, the man is rich).
The second statement describes the noun man — it does the work of an adjective.
A statement used this way, as part of a larger sentence, is called a Clause.

slides.heading: The Clause
bullets: A Clause is a group of words with its own subject and predicate, used as one part of a larger sentence.
It is like a little sentence working inside a bigger one.
In “A man who is rich owns that house,” the clause is “who is rich.”
The whole clause modifies the noun man, doing the work of a single adjective.

slides.text: A Relative Pronoun stands for a word before it and joins a modifying clause to that word.
examples: the man who is rich  (who stands for man)

slides.heading: The Relative Clause & Antecedent
bullets: A Relative Clause is a clause that begins with a relative pronoun:  “the boy who studies.”
It modifies a noun, telling which one:  “who studies” tells which boy.
The word the relative stands for is its Antecedent:  in “the boy who studies,” boy is the antecedent.

slides.heading: Practice — Find the Relative Pronoun
slides.instruction: Name the relative pronoun in each sentence.
items: A man who is industrious will prosper.
This is the house which my father bought.
I gave him all that I had.
He will do what is right.
The knife which you gave me is lost.
A kind boy avoids what injures others.

slides.heading: Practice — Name the Antecedent
slides.instruction: Name the antecedent — the word each relative pronoun stands for.
items: The boy who studies will learn.
The fish which you caught is a trout.
I like a horse that is gentle.
Solomon, who was David’s son, built the temple.
The knife which you gave me is lost.
He is a man that deserves respect.

slides.heading: Practice — Find the Relative Clause
slides.instruction: Name the whole relative clause in each sentence.
items: The book which fell is torn.
A man who lies is not trusted.
The cake that Mom baked is gone.

slides.heading: Who, Which, or That?
bullets: Use who for persons:  “the girl who sings.”
Use which for animals and things:  “the dog which barks,” “the book which fell.”
Use that for either persons or things:  “the man that spoke,” “the house that stood.”
what means “that which”:  “He does what is right” = “the thing that is right.”

slides.heading: Practice — Who, Which, or What?
slides.instruction: Fill each blank with who, which, or what.
items: The girl ___ sings is my sister.
The ball ___ rolled away is lost.

slides.heading: Interrogative Pronouns
bullets: An Interrogative Pronoun is used in asking a question:  who, whose, whom, which, what.
“Who wrote it?”  ·  “What did he say?”  ·  “Which is yours?”
When which or what comes before a noun, it is an interrogative adjective:  “Which road?” “What noise?”
So: standing alone → a pronoun; placed before a noun → an adjective.

slides.heading: Practice — Find the Interrogative Pronoun
slides.instruction: Name the interrogative pronoun (the question-word that stands alone).

slides.heading: Practice — Pronoun or Adjective?
slides.instruction: Is the question-word a pronoun (stands alone) or an adjective (before a noun)?

slides.heading: Common Mistakes with Pronouns
bullets: Use I, he, she, they as the subject — not me, him, her, them:  “He and I went,” not “Him and me went.”
After is or was, use I, he, she:  “It was I,” not “It was me.”
Possessive pronouns take no apostrophe — write yours, hers, ours, theirs, not your’s or her’s.
Name yourself last:  “you and I,” “he and I,” not “I and he.”

slides.heading: Practice — Fix the Pronoun
slides.instruction: Each sentence has a pronoun mistake. Give the correct words.
items: Him and me were in the boat.
Me and the doctor were there.
Which is correct: “Him and me went” or “He and I went”?
answers: A word that stands for a preceding word and joins a modifying clause.
The word a relative pronoun stands for.
A clause introduced by a relative pronoun.
A pronoun used in asking a question.
Who, whose, whom, which, and what.
